notes.text: Go to, &c. — It was very natural for a king to suppose, that the king of Israel could do more than any of his subjects.

Elisha sent — Which he did, partly, to exercise Naaman's faith and obedience: partly, for the honour of his religion, that it might appear he sought not his own glory and profit, but only God's honour, and the good of men.
Was wroth — Supposing himself despised by the prophet.
Are not, &c. — Is there not as great a virtue in them to this purpose? But he should have considered, that the cure was not to be wrought by the water, but by the power of God.
My father — Or, our father. So they call him, to shew their reverence and affection to him.

glossa.text: *Naaman,* etc. ((RAB.)) He signifies the Gentiles who bear rule by valour in war and enjoy the beauty of things. Whence Naaman is interpreted "comeliness" or "their commotion": a man valiant and rich, but a leper; because although through the power of his kingdom and the abundance of his goods he seemed to hold dominion: yet through the error of idolatry he appeared foul with leprosy.

*And out of Syria.* ((ID.)) Robbers out of Syria, etc., *as far as* as in the Gospel the prince of the priests did.

((ID.)) And the Lord *whom he foreknew, them he also called,* etc. The Gentile people coming to the house of Elisaeus, etc., *as far as* because the baptized must be confirmed by the partaking of the Lord's body.

notes.text: Cometh — Speedily and in due season.
Mountain — My kingdom: kingdoms are usually called mountains in prophetical writings.
Profit — What wilt thou gain by it? The dust - Shall they that are dead celebrate thy goodness in the land of the living? Or, shall my dust praise thee?

Sackcloth — Given me occasion to put off that sackcloth, which they used to wear in times of mourning, Esth iv, 1 chap. xxxv, 13 Isaiah xxxii, 11 Joel i, 13. Girded - With joy, as with a garment, surrounding me on every side.

My glory — My tongue. David professes his confidence in God, intermixing prayer to him, ver. 1-8. Complains to God and prays for deliverance, ver. 9-18. Concludes with giving glory to God, and encouraging others to trust him, ver. 19-24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *O Lord my God, I have cried to thee,* etc. ((AUG.)) Christ, etc., *as far as* but not in the dedication.
*Into the pit.* ((HIER.)) That is, out of the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest, like them, I should fall headlong into death.
*Confess ye,* etc. ((AUG.)) Because out of his own goodness and holiness, not ours, he was mindful of us.

*For wrath.* ((ID.)) That is, vengeance, by which he avenged upon us the first sin, which by death you have loosed.

*At evening.* ((ID.)) Because wrath, etc., *as far as* that is, in the time of grace after the time before the law and under the law.

((HIER.)) *At evening.* Because, when the Lord had suffered and been buried, the Apostles and the women continued in weeping and groaning. *And in the morning gladness.* Because coming to the sepulchre in the morning they received from the Angels the glory of the resurrection. *Weeping.* ((CASS.)) It shall abide for men who look toward the evening, at which Adam turned aside and went out from paradise: but there shall be gladness for those who look toward the morning, at which Christ rose again.

*But I.* How he acted before the dedication and deserved it. ((AUG., CASS.)) He acts at evening. But I, while abundance was mine in paradise, said: I shall not be moved from this good, believing the devil who said: *Thou shalt not die the death ((Gen. III))* . But, O Lord, in *thy will thou hast given strength to my beauty;* which is, I was good and strong not of myself, but of thee. And that thou mightest show it: *Thou hast turned away thy face,* that is, thou hast sent me forth out of paradise: but now, set here, *I will cry to thee,* etc.

*Thou hast turned away.* ((CASS.)) God turned away his face from Christ, by exposing him to the passion and to death; and thus Christ was troubled: *My soul is sorrowful even unto death. ((Matth. XVI.)) Troubled.* ((AUG.)) Calling to mind that time of trouble and of misery, and set in it, I hear the voice of the head who is to die for me, saying: *To thee, O Lord, will I cry.*

*What profit is there in my blood.* ((ID.)) He shows the necessity by which he does not suffer him to go down into corruption. *Whilst I go down into corruption.* For if I do not rise again at once, and the body is corrupted, I shall announce to no one, I shall gain no one. Confession is twofold, let us never be without it: when it is ill with us in tribulations, let us confess our sins; when it is well, let us confess praise to God in the exultation of justice.
*The Lord hath heard.* ((CASS.)) He treats of how he received it, namely the dedication. He said: I will cry, I will beseech, but the Lord heard me beseeching.

*Thou hast cut my sackcloth.* ((ID.)) Sackcloth is a rough garment, granted for the use of labour or in a time of sadness, as to the Ninivites; that is, human flesh, which was rent by dying: and there came forth the corn of the glorious resurrection, or of the godhead. Or else, the penalty of sin, which being destroyed in the resurrection, the godhead before hidden was brought forth: just as what the sack conceals whole, it opens when rent. ((AUG.)) Sackcloth of goats or of kids is mortality, which Christ drew or took from sinners; whence: *Whilst they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth ((Psal. XXXIV))*, that they might not see what was within.
*I shall not be pricked.* ((ID.)) I shall not now die unto the end. *O Lord God, I will confess to thee for ever.* What is: *I will confess to thee for ever?* For ever I will praise thee.

notes.text: God is not mocked — Although they attempt to mock him, who think to reap otherwise than they sow.

For he that now soweth to the flesh — That follows the desires of corrupt nature. Shall hereafter of the flesh - Out of this very seed. Reap corruption - Death everlasting. But he that soweth to the Spirit - That follows his guidance in all his tempers and conversation. Shall of the Spirit - By the free grace and power of God, reap life everlasting.
But let us not be weary in well doing — Let us persevere in sowing to the Spirit. For in due season - When the harvest is come, we shall reap, if we faint not.

Therefore as we have opportunity — At whatever time or place, and in whatever manner we can. The opportunity in general is our lifetime; but there are also many particular opportunities. Satan is quickened in doing hurt, by the shortness of the time, Rev. xii, 12. By the same consideration let us be quickened in doing good. Let us do good - In every possible kind, and in every possible degree. Unto all men - neighbours or strangers, good or evil, friends or enemies. But especially to them who are of the household of faith. For all believers are but one family.
Ye see how large a letter — St. Paul had not yet wrote a larger to any church. I have written with my own hand - He generally wrote by an amanuensis.

As many as desire to make a fair appearance in the flesh — To preserve a fair character. These constrain you - Both by their example and importunity. To be circumcised - Not so much from a principle of conscience, as lest they should suffer persecution - From the unbelieving Jews. For the cross of Christ - For maintaining that faith in a crucified saviour is alone sufficient for justification.

For neither they themselves keep the whole law — So far are they from a real zeal for it. But yet they desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh - That they may boast of you as their proselytes, and make a merit of this with the other Jews.

But God forbid that I should glory — Should boast of anything I have, am, or do; or rely on anything for my acceptance with God, but what Christ hath done and suffered for me. By means of which the world is crucified to me - All the things and persons in it are to me as nothing. And I unto the world - I am dead to all worldly pursuits, cares, desires, and enjoyments.
For neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision — Neither of these is of any account. But a new creation - Whereby all things in us become new.

And as many as walk according to this rule -

1. Glorying only in the cross of Christ.

2. Being crucified to the world. And,

3. Created anew. Peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel, that is, the Church, of God - Which consists of all those, and those only, of every nation and kindred, who walk by this rule.

glossa.text: *Be not deceived.* As if he should say: Let no one excuse himself in vain, because God cannot be deceived. For he knows your hearts, he is not ignorant of your means. A plausible excuse can appease a man, it cannot deceive God.

To *He that soweth in the flesh* he adds *his own.* But when he says, *in the spirit,* he does not add *his own,* because the carnal seed is from man, but the spiritual seed is from the Spirit of God. But the harvest here is promised at the end. And therefore in sowing there is need of perseverance. *In the flesh, in the spirit. ((AMBROS.))* A Christian man consists of spirit and flesh. For man in comparison with the Holy Spirit is flesh. *But he that soweth.* That is, he who gives to the spirit an offence out of faith, serving justice with charity, and understanding the law spiritually, shall reap of the spirit, etc.

*Let us not fail.* If a man has set no end to his work, neither does God set an end to the reward. As much as we shall have sown in works, so much shall we reap in fruits. And as much as the eagerness of him who seeks shall have enlarged itself, so much shall the hand of him who repays open itself unto the reward, because each shall so receive as he does; because he who shall be strong to sow shall be strong to reap. *For in time.* God does not at once do whatsoever is prayed for unto salvation; nor does he therefore deny because he defers, but he grants it in his own, that is, in a fitting time.

*Whilst we have time.* The time of sowing is the present life through which we run. In this it is lawful for us to sow what we will. But when it shall have passed, the time of working is taken away; whence: *Work while it is day: the night will come when now no one will be able to work ((Joan. IX))* . *Towards all.* Mercy is to be bestowed upon all. Wherein the just, who are of faith, are to be preferred. And that it is due to all our enemies also, who are wicked, persecuting the Church, the Lord is witness: *Do good to them that hate you. Love your enemies ((Luc. VI))*; because they too are men: upon whom in this the Lord rains, and gives the sun.

*But see.* After he has exhorted unto moral works, he returns to that which was treated of before: namely, that legal observances are not to be held. But lest anyone under his name should deceive the incautious, he takes heed, completing the end of the epistle with the notation of his own hand. For from this place he wrote it out with his own hand as far as the end.

*These constrain.* These were the false apostles, who so preached Christ that they taught also that the law was to be kept. They preached the cross, that they might have gain from the faithful; the law, that they might please the Jews. *That for the cross of Christ persecution,* etc. Perhaps he says this for this reason, because the Roman emperors Caius Caesar, and Octavian, and Augustus, promulgated laws that the Jews, wheresoever they were, should live by their own rite and be devoted to their ancestral ceremonies. For whosoever was circumcised, although he believed in Christ, was held as a Jew among the Gentiles; but he who, being uncircumcised, showed forth by his uncircumcision that he was not a Jew, was made liable to the persecutions as well of the Gentiles as of the Jews. Those therefore who had corrupted the Galatians, desiring to decline these persecutions, urged circumcision upon the disciples for a defence. For neither could the Jews persecute them, nor the Gentiles those whom they saw both circumcise proselytes and themselves keep the things of the law.

*The world is crucified to me.* It happens for the most part that a man does not hold the world in his mind, but yet the world binds him fast in its own occupations and the man is dead to the world, and the world as though alive beholds him, while it strives to snatch into its own acts one who is intent on another thing; but neither does Paul desire the world, nor the world him: so that, dead in both, neither of the two beholds the other. Because therefore neither did Paul seek the glory of the world, nor was he himself sought by the glory of the world, therefore he glories that both himself to the world and the world to himself is crucified. *And I to the world.* Neither do I desire anything in the world, nor does it itself recognize anything of its own in me. As the Lord says: *For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing ((Joan. XIV))*.

notes.text: Pray ye the Lord of the harvest, that he would thrust forth labourers — For God alone can do this: he alone can qualify and commission men for this work. Matt. ix, 37.
Matt. x, 16.
Salute no man by the way — The salutations usual among the Jews took up much time. But these had so much work to do in so short a space, that they had not a moment to spare.
A son of peace — That is, one worthy of it.
Matt. x, 11.
The kingdom of God is at hand — Though ye will not receive it.

glossa.text:
*And after these things,* etc. ((BED.)) Just as in the apostles there is the form of bishops, etc., *as far as* just as the sun is wont to accomplish the three-day circuit of its light in seventy-two hours.

*He sent them two and two.* By this, that he sends them two and two, it is intimated that no one ought to take up the office of preaching who has not charity toward another. Or they are sent two by two according as the animals were sent into the ark two by two, that is, male and female, unclean before in carnal generation, but cleansed by the sacrament of the Church through spiritual grace in the preaching of the disciples.

*The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.* The harvest is the crowd of believers; the labourers are the apostles and those who follow them. And although the harvest has been sown by the word of God, still it requires the toil of tillage and the careful service of a labourer, lest the birds of heaven scatter the seeds that have been sown.

*As lambs among wolves.* As the wolf lies in wait for the sheep, so does the heretic for the faithful. And as the wolf goes about the sheepfold by night, not daring to enter, scouting out the dog's sleep, the shepherd's absence or sloth, so the heretic tries to deceive the faithful by the night of his own interpretation, not entering the Church, and strives either to avoid the pastors of the Church, or to kill them, or to send them into exile. The wolf, stiff by the nature of its body, cannot easily bend itself; so the heretic is not wont to call back the purpose of his hard heart from error.

*Carry therefore neither purse nor scrip.* So great ought a preacher's confidence in God to be, that even if he does not foresee the means of the present life, he yet knows most certainly that they will not fail him, lest, while his mind is taken up with things temporal, he preach the eternal things less. *Salute no man by the way.* He bids them make haste and press on, lest they be turned aside from the journey enjoined them by conversation with someone they meet. Nor does he say simply, *Salute no man,* since it is a usage of human kindness to salute others, but he added, *by the way,* because it is not the diligence of greeting that is taken away, but the obstacle that hinders devotion is done away with, so that, when divine things are commanded, human things may be set aside for a little.

*And in the same house.* If your peace be received, it is fitting that you remain in it, receiving carnal wages from those to whom you offer heavenly things. Behold, he who forbade purse and scrip grants means from preaching, yet in such a way that they be content with the food and drink set before them. *Remain.* There must be no removing from house to house with a roving readiness, so that constancy may be preserved in the love of hospitality, lest the close bond of friendship once grown up be easily dissolved. *For he is worthy.* Note that two wages are owed to the one work of preachers: one on the way, which sustains us in labour; another in the fatherland, which rewards us in the resurrection.

*And into whatsoever city.* Having described the various lodging of a house, he teaches what they ought to do in cities as well: namely, to have fellowship in all things with the godly, and to be kept apart in all things from the company of the ungodly.

*Even the dust.* He bids them shake off the dust: either as a testimony of the earthly labour which they undertook for them in vain; or that they may show that to such a degree do they seek nothing earthly from them, that they do not even suffer the dust from their land to cleave to them.

sermons.author: John Wesley

hymns.title: Stand up, stand up for Jesus
Sois la semilla gue ha de crecer (You are the seed that will grow a new sprout)
At the font we start our journey

praise.title: Yet Not I But Through Christ in Me

Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.
echoes.note: "Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (v.7) draws on the wisdom maxim of moral retribution stated in Job 4:8, "those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same." The sowing/reaping figure is a stock OT idiom; volume is high and coherence with Paul's flesh-vs-Spirit harvest (v.8) is strong.

echoes.text: For they sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind. He has no standing grain. The stalk will yield no head. If it does yield, strangers will swallow it up.
echoes.note: Hosea's "they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind" is the prophetic locus for inexorable sowing-reaping judgment, closely matching Gal 6:7-8's certainty that the harvest answers the seed. Recurrence of the agricultural-judgment topos across the prophets supports availability; coherence with reaping corruption is high.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you. You have plowed wickedness. You have reaped iniquity. You have eaten the fruit of lies, for you trusted in your way, in the multitude of your mighty men.
echoes.note: Hosea 10:12-13 opposes sowing righteousness/steadfast love and reaping accordingly versus plowing iniquity and reaping injustice, the same antithetical structure as Paul's sowing to the flesh vs. to the Spirit (v.8). The two-way harvest imagery makes this among the strongest prophetic substrates for the pericope.

echoes.text: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.
echoes.note: "Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity" supplies the sapiential form of the maxim Paul cites in v.7. Volume is moderate and the proverb belongs to the same cluster as Job 4:8; coherence is high though no single source is quoted verbatim.
echoes.lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works.

echoes.text: Wicked people earn deceitful wages, but one who sows righteousness reaps a sure reward.
echoes.note: "Whoever sows righteousness gets a sure reward" matches the positive pole of Paul's harvest ("sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life," v.8) and the promise of v.9 that doing good will reap in due season. Part of the wisdom sowing-cluster; offered as a corroborating echo rather than a single source.

echoes.text: My son, sow not upon the furrows of unrighteousness, And you shall not reap them sevenfold.
echoes.note: "Do not sow in the furrows of injustice, lest you reap them sevenfold" is the Second-Temple form of the maxim, demonstrating its currency in Paul's milieu (availability). Volume is moderate; it strengthens the case that v.7 cites a proverbial commonplace rather than one prophet.

echoes.text: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.
echoes.note: "We will reap in due season" (v.9) may faintly recall the covenant promise of rain and harvest "in its season" for obedience. Coherence with eschatological reaping is partial and the verbal link is thin; marked contested.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: "Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy" parallels v.9's encouragement not to grow weary because reaping comes in due season if one does not give up. The consolatory sowing-reaping reversal coheres with Paul's exhortation, though there is no verbal citation; contested.

echoes.text: Is this the way you repay Yahweh, foolish and unwise people? Isn’t he your father who has bought you? He has made you and established you.
echoes.note: "God is not mocked" (v.7) resonates with the Song of Moses' rebuke of the people who treat the LORD with contempt and with the broader OT motif that God will not be derided. Volume is low and no single text is in view; offered as a faint contested backdrop.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: "Neither circumcision... but a new creation" (v.15) draws on Isaiah's "new heavens and a new earth," the prophetic announcement of God's eschatological re-creation. Recurrence of the new-creation theme across Isaiah and coherence with Paul's crucified-world (v.14) make this the primary OT source for kaine ktisis.

echoes.text: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.
echoes.note: Isaiah 66:22's "new heavens and new earth" that shall remain reinforces 65:17 as the scriptural matrix for the abiding "new creation" of v.15. The pairing supplies recurrence within Isaiah; coherence with Paul's contrast between old marks-in-the-flesh and new creation is strong.

echoes.text: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
echoes.note: "Do not remember the former things... I am doing a new thing" frames the new creation as the displacement of what is old, paralleling Paul's relegation of circumcision/uncircumcision to nothing (v.15). Volume is moderate and the theme is part of Isaiah's new-exodus cluster.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The promise of a "new heart" and "new spirit" undergirds Paul's interior new-creation reality over against fleshly circumcision (vv.12-15). Coherence with the flesh/Spirit antithesis of the chapter is high, though the language is anthropological rather than cosmic; corroborating echo.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will punish all those who are circumcised in uncircumcision: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness; for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's oracle that God will punish all who are "circumcised yet uncircumcised"—Israel being uncircumcised in heart—anticipates Paul's devaluing of fleshly circumcision in favor of inward transformation (vv.12-15). Volume is moderate; the prophetic relativizing of physical circumcision strongly coheres with Paul's argument.

echoes.text: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.
echoes.note: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart" supplies the Torah's own move from fleshly to inward circumcision, the trajectory Paul completes with "new creation" (v.15). Coherence is high and the motif recurs (Deut 30:6); offered as a corroborating echo of the heart-circumcision tradition.

echoes.text: But as for those who turn aside to their crooked ways, Yahweh will lead them away with the workers of iniquity. Peace be on Israel.
echoes.note: "Peace... on God's Israel" (v.16) echoes the psalm's closing benediction "Peace be upon Israel," a liturgical blessing Paul redirects to those who walk by the rule of new creation. Volume and the formulaic shape (peace-upon-Israel) are high; coherence with a closing benediction is exact.

echoes.text: Yes, may you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.
echoes.note: Psalm 128:6 likewise ends "Peace be upon Israel," reinforcing v.16 as a deliberate echo of the Psalter's pilgrimage benediction. Recurrence of the exact phrase across Pss 125 and 128 strengthens availability; Paul invokes the blessing while redefining its recipients.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The Aaronic benediction—"the LORD... give you peace"—is the liturgical fountainhead for pronouncing peace and mercy upon Israel (v.16). Volume of the peace-blessing motif is high though the verbal contact is thematic; coherence with a closing apostolic blessing is strong.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done in its midst. To the others he said in my hearing, Go through the city after him, and strike: don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity; kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is […]
echoes.note: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body" (v.17) evokes the protective mark (taw) set on the foreheads of the faithful who are spared the slaughter. The marking that distinguishes God's own coheres with Paul's stigmata as the true seal over against circumcision; verbal contact is figural but apt.

echoes.text: One will say, ‘I am Yahweh’s;’ and another will be called by the name of Jacob; and another will write with his hand ‘to Yahweh,’ and honor the name of Israel.”
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of one who "writes on his hand, 'The LORD's,'" marking belonging to God, parallels Paul's bodily "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as a sign of ownership. Coherence with the slave-brand/belonging motif is good; volume is moderate and the link is figural.

echoes.text: “You shall make a plate of pure gold, and engrave on it, like the engravings of a signet, ‘HOLY TO YAHWEH.’ You shall put it on a lace of blue, and it shall be on the sash; on the front of the sash it shall be. It shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall make holy in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always on his forehead, that they may be accepted before Yahweh.
echoes.note: The high-priestly gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" worn on the body has been proposed as background for Paul's engraved marks of Jesus (v.17). The cultic-engraving association is suggestive but verbally remote; offered as a contested, low-volume echo.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor tattoo any marks on you. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Torah's prohibition of cutting marks in the flesh forms an ironic backdrop to Paul's embrace of the "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as honorable wounds. The connection is conceptual rather than citational and runs by contrast; marked contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
echoes.note: Jesus appoints seventy and sends them out as bearers of his commissioned authority, evoking the seventy elders on whom God places the spirit that was on Moses. Volume is strong in the precise number seventy and the theme of delegated, Spirit-empowered authority; coherence with Luke's Moses typology (the prophet like Moses, Acts 3) reinforces it.

echoes.text: The two angels came to Sodom at evening. Lot sat in the gate of Sodom. Lot saw them, and rose up to meet them. He bowed himself with his face to the earth, and he said, “See now, my lords, please turn aside into your servant’s house, stay all night, wash your feet, and you can rise up early, and go on your way.” They said, “No, but we will stay in the street all night.” He urged them greatly, and they came in with him, and entered into his house. He made […]
echoes.note: The verdict that it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for the rejecting city invokes the paradigmatic destruction of Sodom as the measure of judgment for inhospitality. Volume and availability are high, and the inhospitality theme coheres exactly with rejecting the sent messengers.

echoes.text: Moses went out, and told the people Yahweh’s words; and he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them around the Tent. Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more.
echoes.note: The gathering and dispersal of the seventy who then prophesy parallels the sending two by two and the later joyful report of empowered ministry. Recurrence of the seventy-elders motif within the same Numbers pericope strengthens the linkage to Luke's mission.

echoes.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance.
echoes.note: The seventy who ascend with Moses to ratify the covenant supply an alternate or supplementary base for the number seventy as a body of authorized representatives of Israel. Availability and the fixed numeral make it a plausible secondary source alongside Numbers 11.

echoes.text: Now this is the history of the generations of the sons of Noah and of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth were: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan were: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. Of these were the islands of the nations divided in their lands, everyone after his language, after their families, in […]
echoes.note: The Table of Nations was reckoned in Jewish tradition as seventy (LXX seventy-two) nations, so a seventy(-two)-fold mission figurally anticipates the Gentile harvest, fitting Luke-Acts' universal scope. The textual variant seventy/seventy-two mirrors the MT/LXX count of the nations, a coherence rarely coincidental.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: The plentiful harvest needing laborers draws on the prophetic harvest as eschatological ingathering and judgment, where the sickle is put in because the harvest is ripe. The agrarian-eschatological coherence with the kingdom drawing near and the Sodom verdict supports the echo.

echoes.text: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
echoes.note: Sending disciples as lambs among wolves inverts Ezekiel's indictment of Israel's leaders as wolves tearing prey, casting the unreceptive towns in the role of predators against God's defenseless agents. The predator-prey coherence and prophetic-judgment context align with Luke's woes that follow.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that Yahweh will thresh from the flowing stream of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt; and you will be gathered one by one, children of Israel.
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of Israel gathered one by one in a threshing harvest offers a salvific (not only judicial) backdrop for the abundant harvest and few laborers. The link is faint, resting on shared harvest-of-the-people imagery rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.
echoes.note: Zephaniah likewise depicts the city's officials as evening wolves leaving nothing till morning, a stock prophetic figure for rapacious leadership menacing the righteous. The recurrence of the wolf-against-flock trope makes it a plausible faint background to lambs among wolves.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Shaking the dust off as a sign-act against the city recalls prophetic gestures of curse and separation, of which Nehemiah's shaking out his lap is a near analogue. The connection is by gesture-type rather than wording, so it remains faint.

notes.text: Consolations — The gospel doctrine was their breasts of consolation. Her glory - Christ was the glory of the people of Israel, though he was also a light to the Gentiles.

Like a river — It is plain this prophecy relates to a farther conversion of the Jews than hath been yet seen. Ye - Ye Jews also. Her sides - The Gentiles were born upon the sides of Jerusalem and dandled upon her knees, as first hearing from the Apostles (who were members of the Jewish church) the glad tidings of salvation.
As one whom, &c. — That is, in the most tender, and compassionate way.

Rejoice — The peace of the church and the propagation of the kingdom of Christ, is always the cause of an heart rejoicing to such as fear God, so that they flourish like an herb in the spring. The hand - The power, protection, and influence of God.

glossa.text: *Rejoice ye,* etc. ((HIER.)) O angels, O apostles, sorrowful for the perdition of the unbelieving Jews, rejoice, comforted by the faith and salvation of the Gentiles, of whom the Church is built.

*That you may suck.* The faith of the simple, and their good works, being delighted thereby. The faith of believers is the milk and the food of preachers. Whence Christ also: *I have meat to eat which you know not ((Joan. IV))*. *And be filled.* The woman in childbed who bore the male child does not lack an abundance of milk in the rearing of the Nation, and of the little ones who were born together, so that she might offer them the two breasts of the Old and of the New Testament. And it is to be noted that the little ones need the milk of consolation, as still living in the flesh: but they who after the milk of consolation have gone forward to solid food shall abound in the delights of truth and of the knowledge of glory of every kind. *That you may milk out.* Holy Church, one in all, in some has milk, that is, simple faith and works. In others there abounds glory of every kind, namely an abundance of charisms, and the knowledge of the divinity and of the humanity of Christ. Holy preachers therefore are delighted in all, as gathering from some this, from others that. *From the breast.* From the apostles and preachers to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or to the doctrine of the Old and of the New Testament. For what they preach they show by their works, so that thus they may afford their hearers a leading.

*They shall caress you.* ((HIER.)) Sustaining you, giving milk, like him who says, *I beseech you, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your hearts ((Rom. XII))* , etc. And: *I beseech you as strangers, ((I Petr. II))*. etc.

*As.* Almighty God, as merciful and pitying, compares himself now to an eagle, now to a hen, now to a caressing sea, that at least by caresses he may allure you. As also the eagle prepares her nest in inaccessible rocks, that access may lie open to none, and in the midst places the amethyst stone, which puts all poisons to flight (according to the natural philosophers, for the keeping off of serpents), and certain other secrets of nature: so he himself places in our hearts a stone, that is, his own faith, namely himself, who is the stone cut without hands from the mountain, by which all the poisons of the devil are put to flight. For the eagle loves her young more than all beasts, and than the beasts of burden, the cattle and the birds, as they say who have written of the natures of living things

*You shall see,* O apostles, the multitude of those living unto the faith. *And your heart shall rejoice* for their salvation, *and your bones,* the virtues, shall spring up in the hearts of others, the fruit of good will and of good working. For as the body is sustained by the bones, so is the soul by the virtues. *And your bones.* In the day of judgment your bodies shall live again in immortality, so that as in the present life you served God with body and soul, so with body and soul you may receive the rewards. *It shall be known.* In the judgment, namely, the Son shall be known as sweet and mild to the good, an avenger and strong to the wicked, he who is the hand of the Father, through whom he works all things

notes.text: All lands — Ye people of all nations. He invites the Gentile world, to the contemplation and celebration of God's works.
We — Our nation, or our ancestors, in whose loins we then were.

glossa.text: *Shout with joy to God, all the earth,* etc. ((CAS.)) First he admonishes all to rejoice over the resurrection of Christ, which gives life to all.

*Give ye glory.* ((AUG.)) Not as the Jews, who give justice to their own merits, and envy the Gentiles their grace. *How terrible. ((Ibid.))* If thou rejoicest, fear also, lest what has been given to the humble be taken away from the proud: as was done to the Jews. Do not therefore insult over the broken branches, but fear, lest perchance he spare not thee either. *Thy works, O Lord.* ((CAS.)) Briefly he calls the mysteries of the incarnation works, that God is man, that he suffered, died, and the like. *In the multitude of thy strength.* ((AUG.)) Here he hints at the resurrection, to which, the lying Jews being shut out, the Gentiles are admitted.

((BEDA.)) The Lord rose again; many believed in him, etc., *as far as* they drank through grace. *They shall lie.* They are works of the earth, which the enemies belie, against those who lie, *let all the earth adore,* etc. ((AUG.)) *They shall lie.* Enemies are wont to lie, etc., *as far as* let all the earth adore.

*Come ye.* ((CAS.)) Diapsalma. He invites beginners to consider the works of God, that one faith may join those whom one reward awaits: where, setting forth those works, he plainly says that the resurrection pertains to the Gentiles *ressurrectionem*, the Jews being repressed.

*Who turneth. ((Ibid.))* The works in which he is terrible, and what they are, he subjoins: *Who turneth the sea.* In the river Jordan according to the letter, mystically in the passing world. *In the river. ((Ibid.))* Although sins are forgiven, yet in the course of mortality they are still there, for immortality is not at once *immortalitai*.

 *In the river.* ((AUG.)) The river is the mortality of the world, where some come and others depart: but he who believes in Christ passes over on foot, humble in himself, not on horseback and proud. *There we shall rejoice. ((Ibid.))* Or thus: The works are terrible, etc., *as far as* and in these Christians rejoice. *In him. ((Ibid.))* When he shall be all in all, or in him who rules, in his own strength.
*Let them not be exalted. ((Ibid.))* On account of the law, as though more were owed to them. *For all have sinned,* etc. ((Rom. III.))

*Bless ye.* ((CAS.)) Diapsalma. He admonishes the Gentiles to bless God, who, although he tries them by tribulations, yet leads them to the kingdom; for these things seem to stand in the way of the promised resurrection. *Make ye heard.* ((AUG.)) Openly, so that he who loves God loves his neighbour also. *The voice of his praise.* Which the Father speaks of the Son: *This is my Son.*

*Who hath set my soul. ((Ibid.))* Here he enumerates for what causes he ought to be preached.

 *For thou hast proved us.* [n: (AUG.)] Thou hast not given us over unto commotion. Because thou hast proved us, thou hast not cast us headlong, thou hast proved us by adversities, by the fire of charity, which does not suffer us to feel torments, or, thou hast tried us by the fire of tribulation, etc.

notes.text: God is not mocked — Although they attempt to mock him, who think to reap otherwise than they sow.

For he that now soweth to the flesh — That follows the desires of corrupt nature. Shall hereafter of the flesh - Out of this very seed. Reap corruption - Death everlasting. But he that soweth to the Spirit - That follows his guidance in all his tempers and conversation. Shall of the Spirit - By the free grace and power of God, reap life everlasting.
But let us not be weary in well doing — Let us persevere in sowing to the Spirit. For in due season - When the harvest is come, we shall reap, if we faint not.

Therefore as we have opportunity — At whatever time or place, and in whatever manner we can. The opportunity in general is our lifetime; but there are also many particular opportunities. Satan is quickened in doing hurt, by the shortness of the time, Rev. xii, 12. By the same consideration let us be quickened in doing good. Let us do good - In every possible kind, and in every possible degree. Unto all men - neighbours or strangers, good or evil, friends or enemies. But especially to them who are of the household of faith. For all believers are but one family.
Ye see how large a letter — St. Paul had not yet wrote a larger to any church. I have written with my own hand - He generally wrote by an amanuensis.

As many as desire to make a fair appearance in the flesh — To preserve a fair character. These constrain you - Both by their example and importunity. To be circumcised - Not so much from a principle of conscience, as lest they should suffer persecution - From the unbelieving Jews. For the cross of Christ - For maintaining that faith in a crucified saviour is alone sufficient for justification.

For neither they themselves keep the whole law — So far are they from a real zeal for it. But yet they desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh - That they may boast of you as their proselytes, and make a merit of this with the other Jews.

But God forbid that I should glory — Should boast of anything I have, am, or do; or rely on anything for my acceptance with God, but what Christ hath done and suffered for me. By means of which the world is crucified to me - All the things and persons in it are to me as nothing. And I unto the world - I am dead to all worldly pursuits, cares, desires, and enjoyments.
For neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision — Neither of these is of any account. But a new creation - Whereby all things in us become new.

And as many as walk according to this rule -

1. Glorying only in the cross of Christ.

2. Being crucified to the world. And,

3. Created anew. Peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel, that is, the Church, of God - Which consists of all those, and those only, of every nation and kindred, who walk by this rule.

glossa.text: *Be not deceived.* As if he should say: Let no one excuse himself in vain, because God cannot be deceived. For he knows your hearts, he is not ignorant of your means. A plausible excuse can appease a man, it cannot deceive God.

To *He that soweth in the flesh* he adds *his own.* But when he says, *in the spirit,* he does not add *his own,* because the carnal seed is from man, but the spiritual seed is from the Spirit of God. But the harvest here is promised at the end. And therefore in sowing there is need of perseverance. *In the flesh, in the spirit. ((AMBROS.))* A Christian man consists of spirit and flesh. For man in comparison with the Holy Spirit is flesh. *But he that soweth.* That is, he who gives to the spirit an offence out of faith, serving justice with charity, and understanding the law spiritually, shall reap of the spirit, etc.

*Let us not fail.* If a man has set no end to his work, neither does God set an end to the reward. As much as we shall have sown in works, so much shall we reap in fruits. And as much as the eagerness of him who seeks shall have enlarged itself, so much shall the hand of him who repays open itself unto the reward, because each shall so receive as he does; because he who shall be strong to sow shall be strong to reap. *For in time.* God does not at once do whatsoever is prayed for unto salvation; nor does he therefore deny because he defers, but he grants it in his own, that is, in a fitting time.

*Whilst we have time.* The time of sowing is the present life through which we run. In this it is lawful for us to sow what we will. But when it shall have passed, the time of working is taken away; whence: *Work while it is day: the night will come when now no one will be able to work ((Joan. IX))* . *Towards all.* Mercy is to be bestowed upon all. Wherein the just, who are of faith, are to be preferred. And that it is due to all our enemies also, who are wicked, persecuting the Church, the Lord is witness: *Do good to them that hate you. Love your enemies ((Luc. VI))*; because they too are men: upon whom in this the Lord rains, and gives the sun.

*But see.* After he has exhorted unto moral works, he returns to that which was treated of before: namely, that legal observances are not to be held. But lest anyone under his name should deceive the incautious, he takes heed, completing the end of the epistle with the notation of his own hand. For from this place he wrote it out with his own hand as far as the end.

*These constrain.* These were the false apostles, who so preached Christ that they taught also that the law was to be kept. They preached the cross, that they might have gain from the faithful; the law, that they might please the Jews. *That for the cross of Christ persecution,* etc. Perhaps he says this for this reason, because the Roman emperors Caius Caesar, and Octavian, and Augustus, promulgated laws that the Jews, wheresoever they were, should live by their own rite and be devoted to their ancestral ceremonies. For whosoever was circumcised, although he believed in Christ, was held as a Jew among the Gentiles; but he who, being uncircumcised, showed forth by his uncircumcision that he was not a Jew, was made liable to the persecutions as well of the Gentiles as of the Jews. Those therefore who had corrupted the Galatians, desiring to decline these persecutions, urged circumcision upon the disciples for a defence. For neither could the Jews persecute them, nor the Gentiles those whom they saw both circumcise proselytes and themselves keep the things of the law.

*The world is crucified to me.* It happens for the most part that a man does not hold the world in his mind, but yet the world binds him fast in its own occupations and the man is dead to the world, and the world as though alive beholds him, while it strives to snatch into its own acts one who is intent on another thing; but neither does Paul desire the world, nor the world him: so that, dead in both, neither of the two beholds the other. Because therefore neither did Paul seek the glory of the world, nor was he himself sought by the glory of the world, therefore he glories that both himself to the world and the world to himself is crucified. *And I to the world.* Neither do I desire anything in the world, nor does it itself recognize anything of its own in me. As the Lord says: *For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing ((Joan. XIV))*.

notes.text: Pray ye the Lord of the harvest, that he would thrust forth labourers — For God alone can do this: he alone can qualify and commission men for this work. Matt. ix, 37.
Matt. x, 16.
Salute no man by the way — The salutations usual among the Jews took up much time. But these had so much work to do in so short a space, that they had not a moment to spare.
A son of peace — That is, one worthy of it.
Matt. x, 11.
The kingdom of God is at hand — Though ye will not receive it.

glossa.text:
*And after these things,* etc. ((BED.)) Just as in the apostles there is the form of bishops, etc., *as far as* just as the sun is wont to accomplish the three-day circuit of its light in seventy-two hours.

*He sent them two and two.* By this, that he sends them two and two, it is intimated that no one ought to take up the office of preaching who has not charity toward another. Or they are sent two by two according as the animals were sent into the ark two by two, that is, male and female, unclean before in carnal generation, but cleansed by the sacrament of the Church through spiritual grace in the preaching of the disciples.

*The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.* The harvest is the crowd of believers; the labourers are the apostles and those who follow them. And although the harvest has been sown by the word of God, still it requires the toil of tillage and the careful service of a labourer, lest the birds of heaven scatter the seeds that have been sown.

*As lambs among wolves.* As the wolf lies in wait for the sheep, so does the heretic for the faithful. And as the wolf goes about the sheepfold by night, not daring to enter, scouting out the dog's sleep, the shepherd's absence or sloth, so the heretic tries to deceive the faithful by the night of his own interpretation, not entering the Church, and strives either to avoid the pastors of the Church, or to kill them, or to send them into exile. The wolf, stiff by the nature of its body, cannot easily bend itself; so the heretic is not wont to call back the purpose of his hard heart from error.

*Carry therefore neither purse nor scrip.* So great ought a preacher's confidence in God to be, that even if he does not foresee the means of the present life, he yet knows most certainly that they will not fail him, lest, while his mind is taken up with things temporal, he preach the eternal things less. *Salute no man by the way.* He bids them make haste and press on, lest they be turned aside from the journey enjoined them by conversation with someone they meet. Nor does he say simply, *Salute no man,* since it is a usage of human kindness to salute others, but he added, *by the way,* because it is not the diligence of greeting that is taken away, but the obstacle that hinders devotion is done away with, so that, when divine things are commanded, human things may be set aside for a little.

*And in the same house.* If your peace be received, it is fitting that you remain in it, receiving carnal wages from those to whom you offer heavenly things. Behold, he who forbade purse and scrip grants means from preaching, yet in such a way that they be content with the food and drink set before them. *Remain.* There must be no removing from house to house with a roving readiness, so that constancy may be preserved in the love of hospitality, lest the close bond of friendship once grown up be easily dissolved. *For he is worthy.* Note that two wages are owed to the one work of preachers: one on the way, which sustains us in labour; another in the fatherland, which rewards us in the resurrection.

*And into whatsoever city.* Having described the various lodging of a house, he teaches what they ought to do in cities as well: namely, to have fellowship in all things with the godly, and to be kept apart in all things from the company of the ungodly.

*Even the dust.* He bids them shake off the dust: either as a testimony of the earthly labour which they undertook for them in vain; or that they may show that to such a degree do they seek nothing earthly from them, that they do not even suffer the dust from their land to cleave to them.

God, you are my refuge and my strength
I looked over Jordan, and what did I see

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.
echoes.note: "Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (v.7) draws on the wisdom maxim of moral retribution stated in Job 4:8, "those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same." The sowing/reaping figure is a stock OT idiom; volume is high and coherence with Paul's flesh-vs-Spirit harvest (v.8) is strong.

echoes.text: For they sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind. He has no standing grain. The stalk will yield no head. If it does yield, strangers will swallow it up.
echoes.note: Hosea's "they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind" is the prophetic locus for inexorable sowing-reaping judgment, closely matching Gal 6:7-8's certainty that the harvest answers the seed. Recurrence of the agricultural-judgment topos across the prophets supports availability; coherence with reaping corruption is high.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you. You have plowed wickedness. You have reaped iniquity. You have eaten the fruit of lies, for you trusted in your way, in the multitude of your mighty men.
echoes.note: Hosea 10:12-13 opposes sowing righteousness/steadfast love and reaping accordingly versus plowing iniquity and reaping injustice, the same antithetical structure as Paul's sowing to the flesh vs. to the Spirit (v.8). The two-way harvest imagery makes this among the strongest prophetic substrates for the pericope.

echoes.text: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.
echoes.note: "Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity" supplies the sapiential form of the maxim Paul cites in v.7. Volume is moderate and the proverb belongs to the same cluster as Job 4:8; coherence is high though no single source is quoted verbatim.
echoes.lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works.

echoes.text: Wicked people earn deceitful wages, but one who sows righteousness reaps a sure reward.
echoes.note: "Whoever sows righteousness gets a sure reward" matches the positive pole of Paul's harvest ("sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life," v.8) and the promise of v.9 that doing good will reap in due season. Part of the wisdom sowing-cluster; offered as a corroborating echo rather than a single source.

echoes.text: My son, sow not upon the furrows of unrighteousness, And you shall not reap them sevenfold.
echoes.note: "Do not sow in the furrows of injustice, lest you reap them sevenfold" is the Second-Temple form of the maxim, demonstrating its currency in Paul's milieu (availability). Volume is moderate; it strengthens the case that v.7 cites a proverbial commonplace rather than one prophet.

echoes.text: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.
echoes.note: "We will reap in due season" (v.9) may faintly recall the covenant promise of rain and harvest "in its season" for obedience. Coherence with eschatological reaping is partial and the verbal link is thin; marked contested.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: "Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy" parallels v.9's encouragement not to grow weary because reaping comes in due season if one does not give up. The consolatory sowing-reaping reversal coheres with Paul's exhortation, though there is no verbal citation; contested.

echoes.text: Is this the way you repay Yahweh, foolish and unwise people? Isn’t he your father who has bought you? He has made you and established you.
echoes.note: "God is not mocked" (v.7) resonates with the Song of Moses' rebuke of the people who treat the LORD with contempt and with the broader OT motif that God will not be derided. Volume is low and no single text is in view; offered as a faint contested backdrop.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: "Neither circumcision... but a new creation" (v.15) draws on Isaiah's "new heavens and a new earth," the prophetic announcement of God's eschatological re-creation. Recurrence of the new-creation theme across Isaiah and coherence with Paul's crucified-world (v.14) make this the primary OT source for kaine ktisis.

echoes.text: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.
echoes.note: Isaiah 66:22's "new heavens and new earth" that shall remain reinforces 65:17 as the scriptural matrix for the abiding "new creation" of v.15. The pairing supplies recurrence within Isaiah; coherence with Paul's contrast between old marks-in-the-flesh and new creation is strong.

echoes.text: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
echoes.note: "Do not remember the former things... I am doing a new thing" frames the new creation as the displacement of what is old, paralleling Paul's relegation of circumcision/uncircumcision to nothing (v.15). Volume is moderate and the theme is part of Isaiah's new-exodus cluster.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The promise of a "new heart" and "new spirit" undergirds Paul's interior new-creation reality over against fleshly circumcision (vv.12-15). Coherence with the flesh/Spirit antithesis of the chapter is high, though the language is anthropological rather than cosmic; corroborating echo.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will punish all those who are circumcised in uncircumcision: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness; for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's oracle that God will punish all who are "circumcised yet uncircumcised"—Israel being uncircumcised in heart—anticipates Paul's devaluing of fleshly circumcision in favor of inward transformation (vv.12-15). Volume is moderate; the prophetic relativizing of physical circumcision strongly coheres with Paul's argument.

echoes.text: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.
echoes.note: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart" supplies the Torah's own move from fleshly to inward circumcision, the trajectory Paul completes with "new creation" (v.15). Coherence is high and the motif recurs (Deut 30:6); offered as a corroborating echo of the heart-circumcision tradition.

echoes.text: But as for those who turn aside to their crooked ways, Yahweh will lead them away with the workers of iniquity. Peace be on Israel.
echoes.note: "Peace... on God's Israel" (v.16) echoes the psalm's closing benediction "Peace be upon Israel," a liturgical blessing Paul redirects to those who walk by the rule of new creation. Volume and the formulaic shape (peace-upon-Israel) are high; coherence with a closing benediction is exact.

echoes.text: Yes, may you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.
echoes.note: Psalm 128:6 likewise ends "Peace be upon Israel," reinforcing v.16 as a deliberate echo of the Psalter's pilgrimage benediction. Recurrence of the exact phrase across Pss 125 and 128 strengthens availability; Paul invokes the blessing while redefining its recipients.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The Aaronic benediction—"the LORD... give you peace"—is the liturgical fountainhead for pronouncing peace and mercy upon Israel (v.16). Volume of the peace-blessing motif is high though the verbal contact is thematic; coherence with a closing apostolic blessing is strong.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done in its midst. To the others he said in my hearing, Go through the city after him, and strike: don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity; kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is […]
echoes.note: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body" (v.17) evokes the protective mark (taw) set on the foreheads of the faithful who are spared the slaughter. The marking that distinguishes God's own coheres with Paul's stigmata as the true seal over against circumcision; verbal contact is figural but apt.

echoes.text: One will say, ‘I am Yahweh’s;’ and another will be called by the name of Jacob; and another will write with his hand ‘to Yahweh,’ and honor the name of Israel.”
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of one who "writes on his hand, 'The LORD's,'" marking belonging to God, parallels Paul's bodily "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as a sign of ownership. Coherence with the slave-brand/belonging motif is good; volume is moderate and the link is figural.

echoes.text: “You shall make a plate of pure gold, and engrave on it, like the engravings of a signet, ‘HOLY TO YAHWEH.’ You shall put it on a lace of blue, and it shall be on the sash; on the front of the sash it shall be. It shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall make holy in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always on his forehead, that they may be accepted before Yahweh.
echoes.note: The high-priestly gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" worn on the body has been proposed as background for Paul's engraved marks of Jesus (v.17). The cultic-engraving association is suggestive but verbally remote; offered as a contested, low-volume echo.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor tattoo any marks on you. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Torah's prohibition of cutting marks in the flesh forms an ironic backdrop to Paul's embrace of the "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as honorable wounds. The connection is conceptual rather than citational and runs by contrast; marked contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
echoes.note: Jesus appoints seventy and sends them out as bearers of his commissioned authority, evoking the seventy elders on whom God places the spirit that was on Moses. Volume is strong in the precise number seventy and the theme of delegated, Spirit-empowered authority; coherence with Luke's Moses typology (the prophet like Moses, Acts 3) reinforces it.

echoes.text: The two angels came to Sodom at evening. Lot sat in the gate of Sodom. Lot saw them, and rose up to meet them. He bowed himself with his face to the earth, and he said, “See now, my lords, please turn aside into your servant’s house, stay all night, wash your feet, and you can rise up early, and go on your way.” They said, “No, but we will stay in the street all night.” He urged them greatly, and they came in with him, and entered into his house. He made […]
echoes.note: The verdict that it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for the rejecting city invokes the paradigmatic destruction of Sodom as the measure of judgment for inhospitality. Volume and availability are high, and the inhospitality theme coheres exactly with rejecting the sent messengers.

echoes.text: Moses went out, and told the people Yahweh’s words; and he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them around the Tent. Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more.
echoes.note: The gathering and dispersal of the seventy who then prophesy parallels the sending two by two and the later joyful report of empowered ministry. Recurrence of the seventy-elders motif within the same Numbers pericope strengthens the linkage to Luke's mission.

echoes.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance.
echoes.note: The seventy who ascend with Moses to ratify the covenant supply an alternate or supplementary base for the number seventy as a body of authorized representatives of Israel. Availability and the fixed numeral make it a plausible secondary source alongside Numbers 11.

echoes.text: Now this is the history of the generations of the sons of Noah and of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth were: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan were: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. Of these were the islands of the nations divided in their lands, everyone after his language, after their families, in […]
echoes.note: The Table of Nations was reckoned in Jewish tradition as seventy (LXX seventy-two) nations, so a seventy(-two)-fold mission figurally anticipates the Gentile harvest, fitting Luke-Acts' universal scope. The textual variant seventy/seventy-two mirrors the MT/LXX count of the nations, a coherence rarely coincidental.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: The plentiful harvest needing laborers draws on the prophetic harvest as eschatological ingathering and judgment, where the sickle is put in because the harvest is ripe. The agrarian-eschatological coherence with the kingdom drawing near and the Sodom verdict supports the echo.

echoes.text: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
echoes.note: Sending disciples as lambs among wolves inverts Ezekiel's indictment of Israel's leaders as wolves tearing prey, casting the unreceptive towns in the role of predators against God's defenseless agents. The predator-prey coherence and prophetic-judgment context align with Luke's woes that follow.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that Yahweh will thresh from the flowing stream of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt; and you will be gathered one by one, children of Israel.
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of Israel gathered one by one in a threshing harvest offers a salvific (not only judicial) backdrop for the abundant harvest and few laborers. The link is faint, resting on shared harvest-of-the-people imagery rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.
echoes.note: Zephaniah likewise depicts the city's officials as evening wolves leaving nothing till morning, a stock prophetic figure for rapacious leadership menacing the righteous. The recurrence of the wolf-against-flock trope makes it a plausible faint background to lambs among wolves.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Shaking the dust off as a sign-act against the city recalls prophetic gestures of curse and separation, of which Nehemiah's shaking out his lap is a near analogue. The connection is by gesture-type rather than wording, so it remains faint.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

doctrine.title: Nicene Creed
doctrine.article: the life of the world to come

registers.label: Spare
lines: You turned our wailing into dancing, and stripped off our sackcloth.
Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes with the morning.
Like Naaman, we washed and were made clean.
What we could not heal in ourselves, God has healed.
The harvest is plentiful; the Lord sends us out two by two.
Peace to this house, and to all who live here.
Come, sing to the Lord and give thanks.
We will praise you, and not be silent. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Imagine Naaman, proud and sick, stepping down into the muddy Jordan once, twice, seven times, and rising with the skin of a child.
Joy comes with the morning.
This is the God who hears us in the long night, who turns our mourning into dancing and unties the sackcloth from our waist.
Joy comes with the morning.
And this God is not done — the fields are white, the laborers are few, and Jesus is sending us out with peace in our mouths.
Joy comes with the morning.
So come up out of the water, shake off the night, and sing. There is dancing to be done and good news to carry.
Joy comes with the morning. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Washed clean in the river like Naaman, we come.
Joy comes with the morning.
You turned our mourning into dancing.
Joy comes with the morning.
The harvest waits; you send us out with peace.
Joy comes with the morning.
Come, sing to the Lord and give thanks.
Joy comes with the morning. Amen.
